issues.issue: The Application is "incorporated herein by reference" but is not attached or described, so what the Employee warranted to be "complete, accurate and truthful" cannot be identified from the instrument. The standard of completeness and accuracy is also unmeasured, which matters because 14.1E makes any breach of a warranty just cause.

The first "Contract Year" runs thirteen months (December 16, 2010 to January 15, 2012), which cannot be squared with the per annum amounts payable "during each Contract Year" in provisions 3.1, 3.9 and 8.4. Whether the first year earns twelve or thirteen months of those payments is left open.

The obligation is only to "meet to discuss" and the University "in its sole discretion — may consider" an extension, so the paragraph creates no measurable duty at all. Whether the meeting requirement is a binding condition or precatory is left to construction.

The salary is stated to be "as compensation for his services to the University and satisfactory performance of the terms and conditions of this Contract," leaving it ambiguous whether salary is conditioned on the University's judgment of satisfactory performance. "Satisfactory performance" is nowhere defined or benchmarked.

The promise of "the standard staff fringe benefits ... as described in the University of Pittsburgh's Staff Handbook" sits against provision 24.2(d), which reserves to the University the right to modify benefits unilaterally without replacing or compensating the Employee. Which controls a reduction in Handbook benefits is unresolved.

The club is only "a mutually agreed upon golf or country club," an agreement to agree with no fallback if the parties do not agree. No cap or standard governs the initiation fees and dues the University must pay.

The University's obligation ends if the Employee "fails or refuses to comply fully with the University's requirements for participation in the program," but those requirements are neither stated nor incorporated. The trigger is therefore fixed unilaterally by one party.

"[T]he same condition existing at the time of receipt ... reasonable wear and tear excepted" gives no ascertainable standard for when the car has not been maintained. Compliance turns on an undefined comparison of condition over time.

"[A]ll Operating expenses ... including without limitation, gasoline and oil" is a catch-all followed by two consumable specifics, leaving unclear whether repairs, maintenance or insurance fall on the Employee. Provision 3.4 separately says the car is "fully insured by the University," sharpening the scope question.

The records to be kept are only "any and all written records concerning the use of the automobile as may be required by the University," an obligation whose content the University defines at will. What records exist to be produced is therefore indeterminate.

The forfeiture turns on whether "the University reasonably determines" non-compliance, a self-judging standard with no stated review. The phrase "any of the above-stated requirements" also sweeps in 3.4(1)'s program requirements, which are not stated in the Contract.

The tickets are given "at no cost" but "all of which shall be used for his official responsibilities," while provision 10.1D expressly contemplates the Employee reporting income from "complimentary ticket sales" as outside athletically related income. The two cannot readily both be given effect.

Reimbursement is limited to "appropriate travel and out-of-pocket expenses reasonably incurred," with "appropriate" and "reasonably" left undefined and the University's "standard procedures" not incorporated. What qualifies is therefore contestable item by item.

The bonus schedule is mechanically broken: subparagraph A offers "the greatest of" three options of which two are the identical $100,000, the second bonus paragraph carries no letter, and the connectors shift between "or" and "and," so whether A, B and C are cumulative or alternative is unclear. The clause also rests on undefined benchmarks such as games "generally considered a part of the national Bowl Championship Series."

Provision 3.8 gives the University the "sole and exclusive right" to commit the Employee to endorse or consult for shoe, apparel and equipment makers, while provision 10.1D expressly contemplates the Employee having "endorsement or consultation contracts with athletic shoe, apparel or equipment manufacturers" whose revenue he retains. The two allocations of the same opportunity conflict.

The $150,000 is payable "in two (2) equal installments" on September 1 and January 1, yet for the thirteen-month first Contract Year the text says only "(by January 1, 2012 for the first Contract Year)," leaving unclear whether one or both installments, and how much, are due then. The payment is also conditioned on the Employee "representing the University as Head Football Coach," without saying what happens on mid-year termination.

The paragraph appears in provision 3.9 but grants the publicity rights "[i]n relation to the subject of, and the matters described in, this provision 3.8," a cross-reference to a different numbered provision. The mislabel makes the scope of the consent uncertain.

The box is provided "[s]ubject to the facility owner's standard conditions," terms of a third party (Heinz Field) that are neither stated nor limited. The University's obligation is thus defined by a document outside the Contract.

The requirement to devote "his full time, attention and energies" is qualified only by "any exceptions hereinafter expressly described," yet provisions 9.0 (his own football camps) and 10.1 (permission to contract independently with outside sources) allow substantial outside activity. How much outside activity is compatible with the full-time covenant must be worked out between them.

The evaluation is to take into account "prior performance evaluations of the Employee and the expectations and goals previously agreed upon by the Employee and the University's Director of Athletics," neither of which existed when this Contract was signed. The criteria for evaluating him are therefore undetermined.

The enumerated duties close with "(9) such other duties as assigned from time to time by the University's Director of Athletics," an open-ended catch-all sitting against eight specific duties. Because 14.1E makes breach of any duty just cause, the outer boundary of item (9) matters.

Provision 5.4 subjects NCAA violations to "disciplinary or corrective action as set forth in the provisions of the NCAA enforcement procedures, including ... termination of employment for significant or repetitive violations," while 14.1B makes any violation of NCAA Rules just cause for immediate termination. Whether termination requires a significant or repetitive violation cannot be answered from either alone.

"[P]roper regard for the academic welfare of the student-athletes" and "fully consistent with the academic standards and policies of the University" import unstated, unilaterally set standards. Breach of this duty feeds 14.1E, so its vagueness has consequences.

The declaration that "[o]verall athletics policy shall remain the exclusive prerogative of the University" stands against provisions 7.1 and 12.1, which give the Employee input on Team operations and authority to hire, set salaries for and dismiss football staff. Where policy ends and the Employee's reserved authority begins is unresolved.

The University need only "permit the Employee to offer input," and the list of subjects ends with the catch-all "other matters pertaining to the operation of the Team," so the provision imposes no measurable obligation and no boundary. Final authority is reserved wholly to the Director of Athletics.

The Employee's availability is owed "at such times and places as the University may reasonably require," with no cap on frequency or duration and "reasonably" undefined. The fund-raising duty is expressly open-ended ("may include, but shall not be limited to").

The defined term "Programs" reaches any show distributed by "any other media" whose subject is "in whole or in part" the Team or University athletics, an unbounded definition. Because 8.3 bars appearances on "competing" shows and 8.4 assigns all Program revenue to the University, that boundary matters.

"[A]ny competing shows or programs" is undefined — it is unclear whether it means shows competing with the University's Programs, with its designee's business, or any media appearance at all. "[S]uch reasonable services as may be requested" is likewise unbounded and may be fixed by a third party's contract the Employee has not seen.

Whether the $350,000 media payment counts as "salary" for the rest of the instrument is unsettled: 3.2 excludes all income other than base salary from benefit calculations, and 14.2 fixes liquidated damages at $750,000 per Contract Year without saying whether this payment is included. The clause's conditional opening ("while the Employee is representing the University as Head Football Coach") sharpens the question on termination.

The two "equal installments" are due September 1 and January 1, but for the thirteen-month first Contract Year the only date given is "(by January 1, 2012 for the first Contract Year)," leaving the number and size of first-year installments unclear. Nothing states how the amount is prorated if employment ends mid-year.

The grant of publicity rights is left unfinished in the instrument and, as written, states no duration or post-termination limit on the University's right to use the Employee's name and likeness. Its relationship to the identical grant in provision 3.9 is also unstated.

The provision begins mid-sentence ("form acceptable to the University; naming the University as an additional insured"), so the obligation it qualifies — the insurance the Employee must carry and its limits — is missing from the text. What is required to be "acceptable to the University" cannot be determined from the words.

The Employee "shall not unreasonably withhold consent when reasonable alternative facilities are offered," with no standard for what alternatives are reasonable, and the University may change arrangements on ninety days' notice with no liability even where the ten-month consultation has been honored. The interplay of the notice route and the consent route is unclear.

"[T]erms and conditions consistent with those then established by the NCAA for the operation of college football camps" incorporates an external, changing body of rules without identifying it. What the University actually owes the Employee is therefore not fixed by the Contract.

The University may demand "such accurate and complete financial, and other, records concerning such camps as the University may, from time to time, request" within ten days, while provision 10.1D treats camp income as the Employee's own outside revenue reportable only annually. The two reporting regimes for the same activity are hard to square.

The University is "released from all obligations relating thereto" on termination, which sits against provision 9.2's promise not to change agreed camp facility arrangements without ninety days' notice or consent. Whether an already-committed camp survives a termination is left unresolved.

The second sentence — "Without limiting the foregoing, the Employee shall be permitted to contract independently with outside sources" — reads as a grant of permission introduced by words of non-limitation, contradicting the blanket prohibition in the first sentence. Whether outside endorsement contracts are forbidden or merely subject to approval turns on that mismatch.

Use of University facilities requires "a separate written contract for the same on terms and conditions acceptable to the University," an agreement to agree with no standard limiting the University's refusal. The provision also duplicates and does not align with the approval requirement in 9.1 for camp use of facilities.

"[S]hall not interfere with the full and complete performance by the Employee of his duties" states no measurable threshold of interference. Read with the full-time covenant in 4.1, it is unclear what outside activity level is permitted.

The statement that changes in NCAA, conference or University rules "shall automatically apply to this Contract without the necessity of a written modification" cannot be squared with provision 24.1, under which the Contract "shall not be released, discharged, amended or modified in any manner, except by an instrument in writing signed by both of the parties." Which governs a unilateral University policy change is unresolved.

The indemnity reaches claims "associated with" the Employee's outside activities, a connector far looser than causation and with no stated boundary. Its overlap with the separate NCAA indemnity in 24.7 leaves the scope of each unclear.

The Employee is "entitled to retain all revenue generated by such outside activities," including expressly "television and radio programs and endorsement or consultation contracts with athletic shoe, apparel or equipment manufacturers," yet provisions 3.9 and 8.4 make all such revenue "the sole and exclusive property of the University." The same revenue streams are assigned to both parties.

"[C]orporate opportunities of the University" and "any activity causing a conflict of interest with his University employment" are undefined terms applied to a university employer. Because 14.1E makes breach just cause, the absence of any boundary is consequential.

Approval of outside income must be "consistent with the University's polices then in effect," policies that are not identified, not attached, and changeable by the University alone. Whether such later policies bind the Employee runs into the written-amendment requirement of 24.1.

The twenty-day vacation entitlement exists only "so long as the timing of use of any such vacation is approved, in advance, by the University's Director of Athletics," with no standard constraining approval. Read with 11.1's forfeiture of unused time, the entitlement can be defeated by withholding approval.

The parenthetical "(for example during a renewal term of this Contract, if any)" does not fit the sentence it modifies — a prohibition on retaining vacation after expiration cannot be illustrated by carryover into a renewal term. The mechanical mismatch obscures whether carryover into an extended Term is barred.
